CATHAY HOTEL
SHANGHAI
MARCH 2, 1933
Dear Family;
This is my first letter to Dauphin's Island, and I hope that in due course
of time it will reach you there.
There has been no
mail from home since Feb. 22 nd
so of course I donot know whether you are going to be South or not.
You can tell the Bacons that the Canadian Pacific Steamship Co. is now
serving "shrimp a la Seafort Inn" when ever the Empress of Asia can get any real
fresh shrimp.
We had some awfully good shrimp when we got to Japan, so I asked the
Dining Room steward if he could have some cooked the way we had them at Dauphin
Island. Groeger and I had them that way, told some of the other passengers, and
as a result this dish became very popular. The steward told me they would continue
o serve the shrimps that way and would call the style as I have written it above.
I am still
waiting for certain developments in New York before going ahead
with negotiations here. In the mean time there is plenty to be done in the way of
gathering all sortd of information regarding the principal cities to be served in
case operations are begun, what the facilities are for landing, type and kind of
surface competition, train and boat schedules, accommodations, time in transit,
amount of first class passengers and first class mail moving betseen certain
points,
etc, etc. Groeger is of course halping on all this, and has just returned
from a trip
to Peiping (Peking) which he made by boat going and by air coming b
back so that he could study the water
service, harbor facilities, etc. He says
that Peiping is very interesting now with all
the excitement.
He met Marshall
Changs pilot who is an old barnstorming flier
who used to be in some of Bill Rob-
ertson's air shows at Lambert Field. His name is Perry Hutton. The character of
the old man in The Good Earth is supposed to be the father of Chang, and the lat-
ter is Sons. Hutton, another American pilot and two American mechanics are living
in the best hotel in Peiping with fat
salaries and all expenses paid. Groeger
said they were a very clean wholesome lot of typical American boys who are reap-
ing a harvest out of the necessities of Chang's military "face". They do not have
much flying to do, and so with the help of a legion of Chineses coolies they keep
the Ford Trimotors looking as though they had just come from the factory.
Last night Col.Jouett called me up and asked me to join a party he
was giving at the Jai Ali. The Chinese have gone crazy over that game, and they
have some
of the best of the Spanish, mexican and Cuban players come over here.
Col. Jouett's mother,
Mrs.J and Mrs. Christy Matthison were on the party. The
latter is the widow of the famous baseball pitcher and mother of the boy whom you
have probably read about who had such a bad smash over here with a Sikorsky. Poor
fellos, he is in the hospital where he has been dangerously or rather hanging to
life by a thread for several maths. His bride of a week was killed in the crash.
The mother is most attractive - very much of a lady and unusually nice looking.
Col.Jouett is a great friend of lots of people we know. He went to West Point
with Tom Lanphier,
is a great friend of Hy.Breckinridge, and said he knew old
Col. Paeglo gott damp vell.
He told a great story on Col. Paeglo. At one of the
stations the old Col.
was giving the offivers a talk. He said
that in the old
days it was always possible to give any instructions and you would be sure that
the same would be carried out with dispatch and with perfection,
but that now
that was all changed. He added
"gott damp now ven I vant some damp fool to do
somedings I have to do it myself. Must write Doc.Lambert that story. Mrs. Jouett
asked me if I happened to know Gentry Shelton. Her remarks were not entirely
sympathetic and as a result I sais "you sound as though Gent had handed you one
of his rubber chacks". She HatHa
said that was exactly what had happened. They
had entertained him, and she said you know the
salary of an Army officer is not
one that permits of much luxury. After accepting their hospitality Gent got them
to cash a check, which of course came back with
the
title which so many banks
have bestowed on Gent's checks of I.S.F. or more probably the other title of N.A.
which describes both Gent and his checks - No Account. We had a lot of fun and
all of us made money betting on the games which are so crooked that we bet on
the players who in previous gamed had been what
Bo would call
"Lousey". After
everyone had placed their bets on other players ours would come to life and win.
I have just this minute received Ma's letter number three of Feb.4th
and also one from each of the girls - big girls. My it was a traat to have those
letters - the first, as I said above, since Feb. 22, and betterstill because they
were unexpected. No boat is due from the States until tomorrow - it must have
come in ahead of schedule. All my love to you - no copies
of this to anyone else.
Know you art all having a
one he and that wores four her makes late
I headway on the tarasust and
Cable me to
quit work and be come i must
Bix
